source: FindMyPast — British Army Lists & Commission Registers 1661-1826; British Army Officer Promotions 1800-1815 (© Chris Daniell), each citing the London Gazette; Kent Burials (Medway Archives); Kentish Gazette and Kentish Weekly Post via FindMyPast newspapers
lede: This archive has carried Robert D'Arcy's career on the authority of Connolly's Roll of Officers of the Corps of Royal Engineers — a book printed in 1898. Every step of it can now be cited to the London Gazette instead, with issue and page, and it begins two years earlier than anything else here.

career.note: His first commission, and now the earliest record of him anywhere in this archive — a year before he married at Portsea and two before his son was christened there.

career.became: At the SIEGE OF FORT ST PHILIP'S, MINORCA
career.src: Whitworth Porter, History of the Corps of Royal Engineers (1889), p. 209
career.note: Under Lieutenant-Colonel Brewse, Chief Engineer in the island, with Captain Gilbert Townshend and Lieutenants Johnston, Douglas, Shipley and Fiddes. The Duc de Crillon landed on 19 August 1781 and the garrison was about three thousand. The first record of him on active service anywhere.

career.became: In BARBADOS — and now confirmed by the Corps
career.src: St Michael, Barbados — christenings of CONSTANTINE (18 Feb 1786) and JANE (17 Mar 1788), father Robert, mother Jane; AND Porter's History of the Corps of Royal Engineers, station list: “Robert D'Arcy, Barbados”
career.note: No longer an inference. The christenings put him in the West Indies with his wife in the middle of the 1780s; the Corps' own station list says the posting outright. What this page said until 15 September 2026 — that these were “the only two records that fall inside” the blank between 1778 and 1802 — was wrong: Porter puts him at the siege of Fort St Philip's on MINORCA in 1781, three years after his first commission.

career.became: COLONEL, and named with his corps for the first time
career.src: Oxford University and City Herald, 1 November 1806 — his daughter's marriage: “MISS D'ARCY, ELDEST DAUGHTER OF COL. D'ARCY, OF THE ROYAL ENGINEERS”
career.note: THE EARLIEST RECORD THIS ARCHIVE HAS FOUND THAT NAMES ROBERT D'ARCY'S CORPS, and it was sitting in the report of a wedding the archive has held since it read the Chatham register. The Chester Courant of 11 November adds the church and the officiant — Chatham Church, by the Rev. I. T. Jones. He was gazetted Lieutenant-Colonel in March 1805; a paper calling him Colonel in 1806 is a newspaper rounding up, which they did constantly, so the rank here is worth less than the corps.

The SAME Ordnance Office announcement, printed on the SAME page of the Gazette and in the same column of the Limerick Gazette, the Kentish Gazette and the Kentish Weekly Post, promoted his son CONSTANTINE D'ARCY to first lieutenant of the same corps. The archive found this page in July and read the father's line without noticing the son's.

career.became: Colonel in the Army by Brevet
career.src: War Office, 7 June 1813 — by the Prince Regent

career.note: Found in the Gazette itself before the subscription was opened.

career.src: Hampshire Chronicle, 24 March 1823 — his wife's death notice: “At Chatham, MRS. D'ARCY, THE WIFE OF MAJOR-GEN. D'ARCY, OF THE ROYAL ENGINEERS”
career.note: Connolly's Roll gives him Major-General on 12 AUGUST 1819 and this archive carried that on the authority of a book printed in 1898. A contemporary newspaper now corroborates it four years later, and gives the corps at the same time.

career.unit: late of the Corps of Royal Engineers
career.note: Died at Chatham and was interred there with military honours on the 19th.

span: Forty-nine years from a practitioner engineer's commission to a major-general's grave.

joseph.head: And his son went to the guns, not the sappers.
joseph.body: Joseph D'Arcy — baptised at Portsea in March 1780, son of Robert and Jean — appears in FindMyPast's British Army, Royal Artillery Officers 1716-1899 from 1795, in the Army List of 1798, in the Commission Registers in 1802, 1803 and 1826, among the officer promotions of 1803, 1804 and 1806, and in the Army Lists of 1840, 1841, 1843 and 1844.
joseph.means: Commissioned at about fifteen and still listed at sixty-four. The Royal Artillery, not his father's Corps of Engineers. The detail of those entries is behind a further paywall even on a trial — the index is visible and the transcripts are not — so this is a career sketched from a list of dates rather than read.

notHim: One entry was discarded. A Robert D'Arcy is gazetted CORNET BY PURCHASE in the 17th Regiment of Light Dragoons on 19 May 1804, described as “Gent”, vice Harris. That is a young man buying his first commission in a cavalry regiment in 1804 — while this Robert D'Arcy had been a major since 1802 and was a lieutenant-colonel by the following March. Same name, different man, and the sort of thing that quietly wrecks a career chronology if nobody looks at the rank.

post.head: And a post, not just a rank.
post.body: The Kentish Gazette of 14 May 1805, reporting the death of his son, calls him “COL. D'ARCY, CHIEF ENGINEER OF CHATHAM LINES”. The Chatham Lines were the bastioned fortifications thrown up to defend the dockyard and the Medway — the largest engineering work in Kent. Every other record of Robert D'Arcy gives a rank. This one gives him a job.

porter.head: The Corps wrote its own history, and he is in it five times
porter.lede: Whitworth Porter's History of the Corps of Royal Engineers was published in 1889 from the Corps' own records. This archive had never opened it. Robert D'Arcy is named at Minorca, in a station list, at Copenhagen, at Walcheren and in the index — which is Porter's own statement that they are one man.
porter.indexLine: D'Arcy, Robert, at second siege of Minorca, 209, 216 ; Copenhagen, 243 ; Walcheren, 248
rows: MINORCA — the siege of Fort St Philip's

“At the death of Colonel Mackellar, Lieutenant-Colonel Brewse had been appointed to the post of Chief Engineer in the island… Under him were Captain Gilbert Townshend, and Lieutenants ROBERT D'ARCY, W. Johnston, J. R. Douglas, C. Shipley, and J. Fiddes.” The Duc de Crillon landed on 19 August 1781; the garrison was about three thousand.
BARBADOS — confirmed from a Corps list, not a christening

A list of First Lieutenants by station carries “ROBERT D'ARCY, BARBADOS” outright. This archive had the posting only as an inference from two christenings at St Michael, and now has it from the Corps.

“The Engineers consisted of LIEUTENANT-COLONEL R. D'ARCY, COMMANDING ENGINEER; Captains B. Fletcher, J. F. Birch, and S. R. Chapman; Second Captains C. W. Pasley, H. Goldfinch, and C. S. Rhodes; First Lieutenant G. Collyer.” The expedition sailed from Yarmouth Roads on 27 July with twenty thousand men under Sir Arthur Wellesley and reached Elsinore on 3 August.

“The Commanding Royal Engineer with this corps was LIEUTENANT-COLONEL R. D'ARCY.” At the siege of Flushing he appears again among the officers summoned: “Colonel Fyers, Commanding Royal Engineer; Lieutenant-Colonels D'ARCY and Pilkington; Captains Rudyerd, Birch, Squire, Pasley…”
porter.gapHead: What it does to the twenty-four-year blank
porter.gap: This page has said that between the commission of 1778 and the majority of 1802 the career is a blank of twenty-four years, and that two Barbados christenings were the only records inside it. That is no longer true. Minorca falls squarely inside the blank, in 1781, three years after the commission — and the Barbados posting is no longer an inference from a baptism register but a line in the Corps' own station list.
porter.arrestHead: And the reason he nearly faced a court-martial

arrest.setup: On the night of 13 August 1809, storming a fleche on the western dyke at Flushing, Colonel Fyers — the Commanding Royal Engineer — was shot in the chest by a musket ball from a hundred yards. It passed first through some inches of sand on the parapet, which is the only reason it was not fatal. Wounded, he ordered that the senior engineer in the trenches deliver him a written report every morning.
arrest.quote: The first morning, Colonel D., an old man beyond sixty, refused compliance, saying he had other things to do, and no solicitation could prevail on him to write a single line… The third morning Colonel D. again declined, saying IT WAS ALL NONSENSE; and on being reasoned with, denied the right of his superior to demand a report from him, because SOME THIRTY OR FORTY YEARS PREVIOUSLY HE HAD BEEN SENIOR TO COLONEL F. He was requested to reconsider the matter, and on a decided refusal the Brigade-Major put him under arrest.
arrest.src: Told by Fyers's own Brigade-Major. Porter's footnote to “Colonel D.” reads, in full: “Colonel D'Arcy.”
arrest.end: “After all the preliminary arrangements for a court-martial had been gone through, Colonel D'Arcy thought better of it, made his apologies, was released, and ever after furnished his report.”
arrest.means: It is the only description of this man's character that this archive holds. Sixty years old, in the trenches, in the third week of the worst British expedition of the war, refusing to write a report for a man he considered his junior — and then thinking better of it.

porter.ageHead: One date it does NOT quite corroborate
porter.age: Fyers's Brigade-Major calls him “an old man beyond sixty” in August 1809. This archive's own best evidence for his age is the Chatham burial register, which gives him as 76 at his death in May 1827 and so puts his birth about 1750–51 — the source the tree's “1751” has always come from. A man born in 1750 or 1751 was FIFTY-EIGHT OR FIFTY-NINE in August 1809, not beyond sixty. The two do not agree, and the register is much the better witness: it was written by a clerk with a date in front of him, while “an old man beyond sixty” is an aside in an anecdote recalled years later by a man complaining about him. It is recorded because it is the only physical description of him this archive has, and because a source that is slightly wrong about an age can still be right about an arrest.
porter.chipAge: an aside, not a birth record — and it misses the register by a year or two
porter.careful: Porter is a nineteenth-century compiler working from Corps records, not the records themselves. He is the Corps' own historian and he indexes all five mentions as one Robert D'Arcy, which is as good as a secondary source gets — but the commission registers, station returns and the Walcheren papers at Kew are the primary evidence behind him, and none of them has been read here.
porter.where: Read 14 September 2026 in the full text of the 1889 edition on the Internet Archive, which is out of copyright and downloads freely.

armylist.head: The 1778 Army List has him, and corroborates Porter
armylist.lede: The printed Army Lists are free and out of copyright. The list of 1778 carries the whole establishment of the Corps of Engineers, rank by rank, and in the junior grade it has him by name.
armylist.entry: Practitioner Engineer and Second Lieutenant: Wm. Kesterman, John Johnson, Charles Holloway, Thomas Whelpdale, John Humfrey, James Fiddes, Richard Hockings, Robert Beatson, ROBERT D'ARCY, Benjamin Slack, James Lees, Geo: Bridges, Lewis Hay.
armylist.means: It is a contemporary printed source for the rank this archive has carried on the authority of a commission register, and it puts him in a seniority run with twelve named contemporaries.
armylist.minorcaHead: And it independently corroborates the Minorca roster
armylist.minorca: Porter, writing in 1889, names the engineers at the siege of Fort St Philip's in 1781: Captain GILBERT TOWNSHEND and Lieutenants ROBERT D'ARCY, W. JOHNSTON, J. R. DOUGLAS, C. SHIPLEY and J. FIDDES. Every one of those six is in the 1778 establishment — Townshend among the Engineers Extraordinary and Captains; Shipley, Douglas and Johnston among the Sub-Engineers and Lieutenants; D'Arcy and Fiddes among the Practitioner Engineers. A list printed three years before the siege, and a history written a century after it, describing the same men in the same corps.
armylist.trapHead: And the question it does NOT settle
armylist.trap: This archive prints two dates for his first commission: 1776, from Connolly's Roll, on the timeline and elsewhere; and 1778, from the British Army Lists and Commission Registers, on this page. The obvious test is whether he appears in the printed lists of 1775 and 1776. He does not — and that proves nothing at all. The men listed beside him in 1778 are not there either: FIDDES, HOCKINGS, HUMFREY and SLACK return nought occurrences in both earlier volumes. Those lists do not print the Practitioner Engineer grade. The absence is the book's, not the man's.
armylist.chipTrap: an empty search, not a null
armylist.resolve: So the two dates stand unreconciled, and the document that would reconcile them is named: WO 54/240, the Board of Ordnance commission book for Engineers, 1755–1780, at Kew, not digitised and not name-indexed.
armylist.where: Read 15 September 2026 in the free full text of the Army Lists for 1775, 1776, 1778 and 1781 on the Internet Archive.
